evidence.title: U11: A standard patent takes a median 980 days to grant; a trade mark 223 days to register
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
For applications filed FY2010 to FY2019, standard patents took a median 980 days (about 2.7 years) to grant, the middle half 681 to 1,318 days. Trade marks took a median 223 days, with a sharp peak at about 222 days; WIPO gives IP Australia's average time from filing to registration in 2016 as 222 days (U70), so the peak matches the office's usual path.

- 99% of standard patents are granted within 2,156 days; 99% of trade marks within 1,081, with a long tail.
- Designs take a median 33 days and second-tier patents 21; an innovation patent was granted after a check of formalities only, so its 21 days are not compared with standard patents'.
- 57 values remain negative (registered before filed), down from 1,497 before the repairs. They are left as recorded.

evidence.text:
Standard patents took a median 2.59 years for FY1990's applications, 2.27 (FY2000), 3.96 (FY2005), 3.49 (FY2010), 2.32 (FY2015), 2.76 (FY2019) and 2.91 (FY2021). Trade marks fell from 2.35 years (FY1990) to 0.60 to 0.69 since FY2005.

evidence.title: U70: The United States files about four in ten patent applications at IP Australia; China now files as many as Australians

section: For analysts: the notebook's own words
evidence.text:
- **IP Australia beside other OECD offices** (2024): 405 patent examiners (median office 83.5) and 134 trade mark examiners (20.5); 347 days from a patent examination request to the first action (median 210); trade marks 37 days from filing to the first action (30) and 97 to a final decision (140); 879,300 trade marks in force (248,300); 69 post-grant patent oppositions (12).
- **The 222-day lead (U11):** WIPO gives IP Australia's average time from filing to registration for trade marks as 222 days (2016), the peak U11 found in IP RAPID. So the peak is consistent with the office's usual path to registration; WIPO's figure is an average, and IP RAPID's mean for FY2010 to FY2019 is 286.5 days (U11).
- **Restated (2 November 2026, pass 8; ADR 0043):** this gave 10,630 for 2005 (from the rounded display) and said the peak was "not an artefact", more than an average can show.

evidence.text:
The steps are not findings; only the last is.

1. For each type and filing year, take the median days from application to registration, among those registered.
2. Convert to years and plot over time.

**Which gives observation U12:** Standard patents took a median 2.59 years for FY1990's applications, 2.27 (FY2000), 3.96 (FY2005), 3.49 (FY2010), 2.32 (FY2015), 2.76 (FY2019) and 2.91 (FY2021). Trade marks fell from 2.35 years (FY1990) to 0.60 to 0.69 since FY2005.

section: Step 3 of 4: How it was prepared (2 steps for this observation, on the IP rights lens)
evidence.text:
2. Standard patents, provisional applications and second-tier (innovation and petty) patents are counted apart everywhere, and headline figures use standard patents.
   - _Why:_ They are different rights. A provisional is a cheap placeholder that is never granted; a second-tier patent is a cheaper, shorter right. Adding them together hides what each is doing.
3. Two placeholder dates are emptied (an end date of 1 January 1970 on 1,282 rights, and one registration before the register began).
   - _Why:_ 1 January 1970 is the "zero" of computer dates, standing in for an unknown date, not a real one.
4. Trade marks registered before 1986 have no "days to registration".
   - _Why:_ The register holds only their filing date, so their recorded time to registration is almost always zero.
5. The "technology area" is kept for patents only.
   - _Why:_ For every trade mark and design it simply repeated the class of goods, so it measured nothing new.
6. An attorney counts only if the agent on record is not the applicant itself.
   - _Why:_ The register's "agent" is the address for service, which is often the applicant's own; counting it said every trade mark had an attorney.

evidence.title: U31: Each right's milestones were added only after five checks of how the register records them
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
Eleven columns of milestones (examination, acceptance, opposition, assignment, extension, lifetime) rest on five checks of IP RAPID's event records. Among them: trade marks' recorded ends fall from 3,213 in March 2026 to 0 from May, probably because an end is recorded only after the grace period for renewal, so trade marks and designs are treated as observed only to 31 March 2026.

- **No separate grant column.** A patent's grant event falls on its registration date for 99.99% of granted patents.
- **Assignments counted once.** 99.78% of patents with an assignment have it published twice, as an assignment and as a party change; the first is used.
- **Only standing events.** 4.76% of patent lapse events were later reversed, and 60.47% of the patents with one are now granted, expired or ceased.
- **When a term starts.** 92.19% of ceased trade marks whose two filing dates differ (mostly international ones) end a whole number of years after the earliest; 84.59% of standard patents ceased since 1996 end 6 to 7 months after an anniversary, at the end of the grace period.

evidence.title: U33: Patent examination stretched to 755 days for FY2006's applications and has been 422 to 516 days since FY2014
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
The median time from a standard patent's examination request to its acceptance rose from 408 days (FY1990) to 755 (FY2006), and has been 422 to 516 days since FY2014. Trade marks went from 666 days to acceptance (FY1990) to 52 to 184 days from FY2005.

- Filing to examination request, standard patents: 192 days (FY2000), 652 (FY2005), 552 (FY2010), 309 (FY2015) and 553 (FY2021). For FY2013 it is 44 days: applicants asked for examination before Raising the Bar took effect, which kept their applications under the old law.
- Certification: 123 to 208 days after grant for innovation patents and 73 to 276 days after registration for designs.
- The latest years are still in progress, so their medians are understated.

evidence.title: B2: The strongest pairs are how the IP system works, not findings, and are recorded but not carried forward
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
The strongest leads are what the filing rules and the way records are made would produce anyway. Australian filers file their international (PCT) applications at IP Australia (strength 0.945), and the inventions they file are made here (0.892). A patent's time to grant rises with how long its owner waits before asking for examination (0.83).

- Each held in the earlier decade too: 0.938, 0.851 and 0.817.
- **The applicant sets part of the pace.** A standard patent's time to grant rises with how long its owner waits before asking for examination; the office is not the only source of delay.
- **A record effect.** Wider families have fewer inventors of unknown country (0.526; 0.582), because Google Patents takes inventors' countries from foreign publications, which narrow families lack (U95).
- **Trade marks:** expedited examination goes with a priority claim (0.78; 0.763), the recording U103 explained.
- **Provisionals:** individuals have no ABN (0.757; 0.738). **Trade marks:** a founding applicant's country goes with its priority office (0.731; 0.774).

evidence.title: B7: Australian organisations' patents took longer to grant than overseas ones in one decade but not the other, so this is not a lead
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
section: For analysts: the notebook's own words
evidence.text: **B7 (observational). Australian organisations' standard patents took longer to grant than overseas organisations' in FY2010 to FY2019, but not in FY2000 to FY2009: not a lead.** Granted standard patents, median years from application: Australian organisations 3.12 against 2.65 for overseas organisations (a difference of 0.476 years, interval 0.435 to 0.52; rank-biserial 0.179), but 3.41 against 3.32 in FY2000 to FY2009 (0.082, 0.044 to 0.123; 0.016). From the examination request the difference is 0.17 years (0.153 to 0.181) in the later decade and -0.079 (-0.099 to -0.057) in the earlier. The route is the candidate third factor: a PCT application's clock starts at national phase entry, about 30 months after its priority (U6), and overseas filers use the PCT most (section 1.5); the screen ties time to grant to the route (0.304; 0.237: claiming an Australian application, a median 1,617 days).

evidence.title: U31: Each right's milestones were added only after five checks of how the register records them
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
section: For analysts: the notebook's own words
evidence.text:
- **When a term starts.** Of ceased trade marks whose earliest filing date differs from their application date (mostly Madrid marks), 92.19% end a whole number of years after the earliest filing date and 1.65% after the application date, so a trade mark's term runs from its earliest filing date. 84.59% of standard patents ceased since 1996 end 6 to 7 months after an anniversary of their date of patent, at the end of the grace period, so a patent's years in force include it.
- **When ends are complete.** Trade marks' recorded ends fall from 3,213 in March 2026 to 776 in April and 0 from May; designs' from 627 in March 2026 to 251 to 399 a month from April; patents run at 1,442 to 1,820 a month throughout. Trade marks and designs are therefore observed to 31 March 2026, patents and plant breeder's rights to 22 October 2026.
- **Left out:** 3,154 events dated 1 January 1970 (a placeholder), and 174 dated before the right's earliest filing (26 of them trade mark oppositions dated 1909), both counts printed above. (Restated 2 November 2026, pass 8; ADR 0043: first given as 171, from build.py's note, which left out 3 trade mark expedite requests the build also drops; the count was not on the page.)

evidence.title: U27: Patent grants peaked in 2016; trade mark cessations reached their highest in 2025
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
Patent grants peaked at 25,687 in 2016, three years after the rush to file before Raising the Bar, and were 19,612 in 2025. Trade mark registrations reached 70,634 in 2021. Trade mark cessations (registered marks let go) rose from 7,240 in 1996 to 35,484 in 2025, the peak, though not steadily: 29,802 in 2019 and 28,319 in 2023.

- Patent expiries rose from 30 (1996) to 4,019 (2025), as patents filed under the 20-year term reach it.
- Ownership transfers: trade mark assignments peaked at 18,370 (2019), patent assignments at 6,015 (2015).
- Trade mark oppositions rose from 824 (1996) to 2,309 (2025, the peak).
- Trade mark cessations fell to 3,773 in 2002 while lapses rose: accounted for by the gap between two Acts' first terms and the large filing year of 2000 (U38).

evidence.title: U29: Forty-two months still stand out after the repairs; each is explained and kept
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
section: For analysts: the notebook's own words
evidence.text:
- **Pauses and their backlogs, kept:** patent grants in June 1991 (113, after the Patents Act 1990 commenced) and in October and November 1998 (248, then 3,373); trade mark registrations in January and March 1996 (0, then 4,021, the Trade Marks Act 1995); patent cessations in December 2006 (82) and February 2020 (7). February 2020 is also the month the innovation patent's phase-out was enacted, but the pause is in cessations of every kind of patent, so nothing in the data links the two.
- **Single low months in steady series:** trade mark registrations in January 1987 (151) and September 1991 (339), design registrations in January 1992 (77), trade mark lapses in October 1986, August 1987 and April 1996 (122, 94 and 243), and patent assignments in February 1992, August 1998, January 2000 and March 2026 (42 to 75); patent assignments were also high in June 1994 (347).
- **A recurring low:** design lapses fall to 0 to 16 in April in six of the seven years from 1996 to 2002, and to 0 in October 2002, in a series of 59 to 76 a month. U39 shows it is how lapses were dated (April's lapses dated in other months), not fewer lapses, and pools those years' months in Stage 2.

evidence.title: Checked against IP Australia
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
- **Stage 1's counts hold up.** IP Australia's own yearly figures are reproduced from Stage 1's data for every kind of right. Standard patent applications agree in all 12 years from 2014 to 2025, within 0.34%; provisional applications within 0.25%; standard patents granted within 0.03%.
- **No observation is contradicted.** 23 are corroborated, 9 are consistent with what IP Australia says, 1 is disputed in part, and 66 cannot be tested because IP Australia publishes nothing comparable.
- **Four things do not agree** (below). Three change how an observation should be read; none overturns one.
- **Two questions close or narrow.** The jump in innovation patents in 2016 (U67) was a real rise that IP Australia reported itself. The fall in first observed trade mark filers (U45) is mostly a fall in linking filers to their ABNs, not in filing.

evidence.title: U28: Around some policy changes filing shows clear rushes, steps and pauses; around others nothing stands out
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
section: For analysts: the notebook's own words
evidence.text:
- **Steps.** Patent expiries fell 98.4% (289.5 to 4.67 a month) when the term rose to 20 years. Extensions of term went from 0.08 a month to 11.17 under the 1999 regime (60 in December 1999, the chart). Second-tier applications rose 71.5% (50.58 to 86.75 a month) when the innovation patent replaced the petty patent. Under the Designs Act 2003, design applications from overseas rose 40.4% and registrations 24.5%; Australians' applications 3.4%.
- **Pauses at commencement.** The Trade Marks Act 1995: no trade mark registrations in January 1996, 4,021 in March (5.5), and Australians' applications at 0.5 times their usual month in January 1996; assignments published rose 79.3%. The Patents Act 1990: 113 patent grants in June 1991, against about 1,025 a month (5.5).

- **US patents often cite Australian research, and R&D spending has fallen.** US patents often cite Australian research institutions' work; 93.6% of those citations come from patents with no Australian applicant or inventor, as most US patents have none. pool.title: U36: Later standard patents are more often still in force at 10 and 15 years; about half of trade marks are still in force after ten years
pool.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
section: Step 4 of 4: From the data to the observation (4 reasoning steps)
pool.text:
The steps are not findings; only the last is.

1. For each granted or registered right, take its years in force from grant or registration, and whether it has ended.
2. Group rights into cohorts by the date their term follows.
3. For each cohort, work out the share still in force after each number of years, counting unfinished rights for as long as they have run (a Kaplan–Meier survival curve); readings with fewer than 30 rights still at risk are left blank.
4. Read off the median and the shares in force after 10 and 15 years. A patent ends on the record six months after the anniversary at which it was not renewed, so "after 10 years" means after the ninth anniversary's renewal; a trade mark ends at the anniversary, so "after 10 years" means after the tenth anniversary's renewal fell due.

**Which gives observation U36:** Of standard patents granted in the 1980s, 53.2% were still in force 10 years after their date of patent; of those from the 2000s and 2010s, 67.5% and 67.3%. The median time in force rose from 10.6 years (1980s and 1990s) to 13.5 (2000s and 2010s). For trade marks the share still in force after 10 years fell, from 67.0% of those filed 1983 to 1989 to 46.9% of the 2000s' and 47.5% of the 2010s'.

pool.title: B6: Patents that Australian individuals file without an attorney are rarely granted, about 36 points less often, in both decades
pool.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
section: Step 4 of 4: From the data to the observation (4 reasoning steps)
pool.text:
The steps are not findings; only the last is.

1. For Australian individuals, find the share of standard patents granted, filed alone and with an attorney.
2. Take the difference, with its interval, in each decade.
3. Repeat among applications whose examination was requested, to set aside those never pursued.
4. Repeat for Australian organisations and for trade marks.

events.answer:
A standard patent typically takes much longer: **a median 980 days from filing to grant**, compared with **223 days from filing to registration for a trade mark**, for applications filed FY2010 to FY2019, according to U11 (Stage 1, descriptive).[1]

The median is the middle wait—not a deadline or a guarantee. For standard patents, the middle half took **681 to 1,318 days**.[2] These timings describe successful applications: U12 (Stage 1, descriptive) notes that only applications later registered or granted count.[3]

The patent wait is not all examination time. B2 (descriptive) notes that applicants set part of the pace: longer waits before requesting examination go together with longer times to grant, so the office is not the only source of delay.[4]

evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
Divisional applications rose from 11.59% to 22.62% of Australian organisations' standard patents between FY2000 to FY2009 and FY2010 to FY2019, and from 7.08% to 15.63% of overseas organisations'. With the field, co-filers and classes held the rise holds (+10.7 and +8.8 points), it holds without the ten filers with the most divisionals, and it holds within the same filers: +19.18 points for Australian organisations, +10.97 for overseas ones.

- **Australian organisations:** +11.0 raw, +10.7 held together (96.9% left). Without the ten filers with the most later divisionals, +7.1.
- **Overseas organisations:** +8.5 raw, +8.8 held together; without their ten largest +8.4. Their ten largest hold 8.51% of the later divisionals.
- So Stage 2's doubling is not a change in the mix of fields or filers: the same organisations file more divisionals.
- Why is not in the data. Stage 2's lead, that a divisional keeps claims pending longer, needs the dates of each divisional's parent and its examination.

evidence.title: What Stage 3 found
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
- **Asking for examination sooner is not a sign of a longer life.** Expedited examination's link with staying in force does not survive the filer, field and route held together, and Australian individuals' expedited patents are about a quarter more likely to end in a given year. On the wider measure IP Australia's commissioned study uses, a request made before any direction (41.39% of granted patents), patents are more likely to end, held together (1.276 and 1.383), against the study's finding. Observations: M5, M40.
- **Some Australian invention ends up owned overseas, by two routes.** Granted Australian-founded patents are more often now held only overseas, at the same reach and filer type, and so are patents filed before the firm's first registration. Inventions made here and filed from overseas come in about equal numbers from international teams and from all-Australian ones. Observations: M6, M27, M30.
- **The same organisations file more divisionals.** Divisionals doubled within the same filers (+19.18 points for Australian organisations, +10.97 for overseas ones), not through a change in fields or filers. Observations: M26.

Strength: Observational, about 65 to 84 institutions (a lead) Questions: Q2. Next: The sector review of the institutions link (OQ11); commercialisation data by field.
- **Raising the Bar's rush, and Australians' lower level of standard patents after it, hold with trend and season held; the Designs Act's overseas step does not stand apart from a rise in a control.** Observations: U28, B37, M25. Strength: Observational. Questions: Q4, Q5. Next: A design for Q5 around Raising the Bar (who rushed, and what their rushed applications became)
- **Divisionals doubled among organisations' standard patents, within the same filers (Australian +19.18 points, overseas +10.97)** Observations: B15, M26. Strength: Observational, holds. Questions: Q4. Next: How long divisionals keep claims pending, and how they relate to their parents' examination (IP Australia's examination records)

evidence.text:
Things the analysis has found but cannot yet explain. They are kept in view, not explained away. Several are closed or narrowed: IP RAPID's innovation patents in 2016 (U67), by the review against IP Australia; the trade mark expedite fall of November 2018 (U34), by IP Australia's own register (U103); most of the fall in Australian organisations' patents filed only in Australia (B11), by a gap in older records (B55); and about half of the recent fall in first patent filers, by the name match (M12).

- Australians' direct filing of standard patents rose to 28.3% in FY2026 (U90), and provisionals filed in FY2025 were followed up less often, mostly by new and heavy individual filers (B38, M35); both could be priority claims recorded late (OQ18).
- The share of divisional applications about doubled among both Australian and overseas organisations, within the same filers (B15, M26); why is not in the data.
- Firms with a first observed patent fell from 1,167 (FY2021) to 810 (FY2024); innovation patents closed in August 2021 (U45). About half of the later fall is linking (M12).

pool.text:
- **Policy changes broke series as the law required; few breaks show behaviour, and fee changes rarely moved filing.** Seven of eight policy changes moved a series further than any comparison month, but most of those breaks were certain by law. The rush before Raising the Bar is the clearest sign of applicants' behaviour. section: Step 4 of 4: From the data to the observation (6 reasoning steps)
pool.text:
The steps are not findings; only the last is.

1. Start from every standard patent application whose filer has an ABN, credited to that filer.
2. Count each firm's applications. 23,971 firms filed 183,989 standard patents.
3. Line the firms up from most to fewest applications.
4. Take the top 1% of firms in that line and add up their applications.
5. Divide by all 183,989 applications. The result is 55.3%.

No—the evidence points to the **same organisations filing more divisionals**, rather than a change in the mix of technology fields or filers. Stage 3’s **M26 (observational)** found that the rise identified in B15 **holds** after those checks.[1]

A divisional is a new application split off from an earlier application, keeping its date; it often protects a different part of the same invention.[2]

### What changed
M26 found that divisionals’ share of organisations’ standard patent applications rose between **FY2000 to FY2009** and **FY2010 to FY2019**:
- **Australian organisations:** from **11.59% to 22.62%**.[3]
- **Overseas organisations:** from **7.08% to 15.63%**.[3]

### How the explanation was tested
M26 held technology field, co-filers and the number of classes together—comparing applications with those measured characteristics taken into account. The rise remained **+10.7 points** for Australian organisations and **+8.8 points** for overseas organisations.[4]

The rise also remained when the largest divisional filers were excluded, and when comparing changes **within the same filers**: **+19.18 points** for Australian organisations and **+10.97 points** for overseas organisations.[5]

**That narrows the explanation, but does not establish why organisations changed their filing behaviour.** M26 explicitly says the reason is not in the data. The earlier suggestion that divisionals keep claims pending longer still needs the dates of each divisional’s parent application and its examination to be tested.[6] Holding measured factors together is not an experiment; unmeasured factors could still explain the change.

evidence.title: M25: Raising the Bar's rush, and Australians' lower level of patents after it, hold with trend and season held; the Designs Act's step does not stand apart
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
Read as an interrupted time series with each series' trend and season held, Raising the Bar (April 2013) brought a rush of Australians' standard patents (0.605 in logs) and a lower level after it (a step of -0.334, about 28% fewer a month), which then recovers; its controls were quiet but for one small series. The Designs Act 2003's step for overseas applicants (June 2004) does not stand apart: Australians' trade marks, a control, stepped too.

- **Raising the Bar:** a slope of +0.089 a year after the step, a lower level that then recovers. **Overseas applicants:** a rush of 0.352, no step detected (-0.047).
- **Its controls:** Australians' designs, rush 0.049 and step -0.077, quiet; plant breeder's rights, rush 0.206, a small and noisy series. Stage 2's reading holds, with the plant breeder's rights' rush as a caution.
- **The Designs Act 2003:** overseas applicants' designs step 0.391; but Australians' designs step too (0.162), and so do Australians' trade marks (0.251), while Australians' standard patents do not (0.036).

evidence.title: U28: Around some policy changes filing shows clear rushes, steps and pauses; around others nothing stands out
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
In April 2013, the month Raising the Bar took effect, Australians filed 1,044 standard patent applications, 4.41 times their average month in the year before. In August 2021, when the innovation patent closed to new applications, 2,789 second-tier applications came in (4.31 times), then 95.9% fewer a month in the year after. Patent expiries fell 98.4% when the term rose to 20 years.

- **Rushes before a change:** Raising the Bar (Australians 4.41 times their usual month, overseas applicants 2.65 times; in the year after, 34.0% and 7.7% fewer a month) and the innovation patent's closure. Filing also rose after each change was enacted and before it took effect: second-tier applications by 176.4%, Australian standard patents by 45.3%.
- **Steps:** patent expiries (the 20-year term), extensions of term (the 1999 scheme, from 0.08 to 11.17 a month), second-tier applications when the innovation patent replaced the petty patent (+71.5%), and designs under the Designs Act 2003 (overseas applications +40.4%, Australians' +3.4%).

evidence.title: B37: Seven of eight policy changes moved a series further than any comparison month; most of those breaks were certain by law, and few show applicants' behaviour
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
For each policy change, the size of the jump or step in the series it targets was compared with the same measure at up to 72 placebo months, five years either side. Seven of the eight changes moved at least one target series further than any placebo month; the Patents Act 1990 did not. Most of these breaks were made certain by the law or the office's processing (no expiries under a longer term, no applications once a right closed). Those that show applicants' behaviour are the rush before Raising the Bar and, perhaps, overseas applicants' step under the Designs Act 2003.

- **Behaviour: Raising the Bar (April 2013).** Australians' and overseas applicants' standard patents both jumped further than in any of 72 placebo months, and Australians' filing stayed lower in the year after. Series it should not have moved (Australians' designs, plant breeder's rights) did not: 37.5% to 81.94% of placebo months moved as much.
- **Behaviour or administration: the Designs Act 2003 (June 2004).** Overseas applicants' designs stepped up further than in any placebo month; Australians' designs did not step beyond the ordinary (61.11% of placebo months as large).

evidence.title: U27: Patent grants peaked in 2016; trade mark cessations reached their highest in 2025
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
Patent grants peaked at 25,687 in 2016, three years after the rush to file before Raising the Bar, and were 19,612 in 2025. Trade mark registrations reached 70,634 in 2021. Trade mark cessations (registered marks let go) rose from 7,240 in 1996 to 35,484 in 2025, the peak, though not steadily: 29,802 in 2019 and 28,319 in 2023.

- Patent expiries rose from 30 (1996) to 4,019 (2025), as patents filed under the 20-year term reach it.
- Ownership transfers: trade mark assignments peaked at 18,370 (2019), patent assignments at 6,015 (2015).
- Trade mark oppositions rose from 824 (1996) to 2,309 (2025, the peak).
- Trade mark cessations fell to 3,773 in 2002 while lapses rose: accounted for by the gap between two Acts' first terms and the large filing year of 2000 (U38).

evidence.title: What Stage 3 found
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
- **Across countries and industries, patents follow business R&D.** Across OECD members, patenting at home follows business R&D at the same income and size; across industries, patents allocated per business follow business R&D at the same value added. Australia is nearest Norway, New Zealand and Sweden on non-IP indicators. Observations: M17, M18, M22.
- **Institutions: research that patents cite goes with their own patenting; licence income does not follow patents.** Across every kind of institution, with kind and size held, research that patents cite goes with more patents per work. At the same research spend, more patents are not seen to go with more licence income. Observations: M38, M24.
- **Raising the Bar's rush holds; the business cycle barely shows.** With trend and season held, Raising the Bar's rush and Australians' lower level of patents after it hold, while the Designs Act's step does not stand apart from a control. With block resampling, the cycle shows only in overseas applicants' trade marks before 2008. Trade marks share a long-run path with real GDP and run a quarter ahead of it, as IP Australia's note finds, but the lead is small once GDP's own growth is held and is not detected since 2008. Observations: M25, M36, M19, M39.

evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
- **Australians, above all individuals, often file without an attorney.** Overseas filers use an attorney for 99.0% of standard patents, Australian filers for 85.4%, and Australian individuals file 62.4% of their trade marks alone. Observations: U20, U48.
- **Provisional applications doubled in FY2026.** 10,069 against 4,143 to 5,047 a year before, mostly from individuals but from organisations too, both broadly and through a few heavy filers. It is in the filings, not the recording. Why is a question for IP Australia. Observations: U8.
- **Around some policy changes, filing shows clear rushes, steps and pauses.** Rushes to file before a rule changed (Raising the Bar, 4.41 times Australians' usual month; the innovation patent's closure, 4.31 times), steps, and pauses when new Acts began; around other changes nothing stands out. These timings are the raw material for the natural experiments the later questions need. Observations: U28, U3.

evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
section: Step 4 of 4: From the data to the observation (3 reasoning steps)
evidence.text:
The steps are not findings; only the last is.

1. For each date column, find the earliest and latest date and the day with the most rights.
2. Compare the busiest days with the dates of policy changes in the policy register.
3. Count rights with no application date, and what else is known about them.

**Which gives observation U3:** The most common application date is 12 April 2013 (1,856 rights), the Friday before the Raising the Bar reforms took effect. The most common earliest filing date is 25 August 2021 (1,342 rights), the day before innovation patents closed. 50,763 rights have no application date: 50,711 patents, 45 designs, 6 plant breeder's rights and 1 trade mark.

- Applications run from 13 February 1904 to 17 October 2026.
- 14 end dates fall after the corpus was built (22 October 2026), the latest on 27 April 2029; they are left as recorded.
- Of the 50,711 undated patents, 50,488 are standard patents, almost all of unknown origin (50,442) and unknown status (49,737); 203 were ever registered (202 of them second-tier). They are old records that cannot be placed in time, so counts by year leave them out: 2.9% of patents. 11,098 design records with nothing in them are dropped (U104).

evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
- **Policy changes broke series as the law required; few breaks show behaviour, and fee changes rarely moved filing.** Seven of eight policy changes moved a series further than any comparison month, but most of those breaks were certain by law. The rush before Raising the Bar is the clearest sign of applicants' behaviour. Of the changes in fees to obtain a right, only one break went the way a price would; of the changes in renewal fees, only one (trade marks, July 1993) survives every check. Observations: B37, B47, B49.
- **Women's share among inventors varies by field more than by filer.** From 4.2% in civil engineering to 26.9% in biotechnology, an order that holds across decades. On provisional applications, Australian organisations' inventors include more women than Australian individuals'. Observations: B17, B18.
- **Across industries, the patents allocated by technology follow R&D once services are counted.** Industry counts are applications allocated by what they protect, not what each industry's businesses file. Through the crosswalk with services, patents allocated per business follow business R&D per business. A division's share of innovating businesses showed no clear pattern with patenting in three surveys. Observations: B53, B54, B42, B60.

evidence.title: U33: Patent examination stretched to 755 days for FY2006's applications and has been 422 to 516 days since FY2014
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
The median time from a standard patent's examination request to its acceptance rose from 408 days (FY1990) to 755 (FY2006), and has been 422 to 516 days since FY2014. Trade marks went from 666 days to acceptance (FY1990) to 52 to 184 days from FY2005.

- Filing to examination request, standard patents: 192 days (FY2000), 652 (FY2005), 552 (FY2010), 309 (FY2015) and 553 (FY2021). For FY2013 it is 44 days: applicants asked for examination before Raising the Bar took effect, which kept their applications under the old law.
- Certification: 123 to 208 days after grant for innovation patents and 73 to 276 days after registration for designs.
- The latest years are still in progress, so their medians are understated.

pool.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
section: For analysts: the notebook's own words
pool.text: - **Who asks, and for what (S2 L1 R35):** 0.84% of overseas organisations' examined patents were expedited in FY2003 to FY2009 and 8.0% from FY2010; Australian individuals 19.71% and 19.95%. By year of request, the share rose in 2011 and 2012 for every kind of filer (Australian organisations 24.85% and 41.26%; overseas organisations with neither a US nor a Japanese priority 23.98% and 32.64%), then fell back. From 2014 overseas organisations' patents with a Japanese priority rose from 1.53% (2013) to 7.98%, and with a US priority from 3.07% to 6.77%, and stayed there. The 2014 rise coincides with the Global Patent Prosecution Highway (6 January 2014), under which an applicant whose claims another office has allowed asks for accelerated examination; IP RAPID records such a request as expedited examination. So "expedited" mixes urgency with work-sharing, which follows examination abroad and would be expected to go with grant and a longer life. The 2011 and 2012 rise came before Raising the Bar (15 April 2013); its cause is not shown.

events.answer:
**There was a clear rush of patent filings around Raising the Bar, and it survives the atlas’s stronger checks—but the evidence is observational, not proof that the reforms caused it.** M25 finds that the rush remains after allowing for the underlying trend and seasonal filing patterns. [1]

Raising the Bar tightened Australia’s patent law from 15 April 2013; applicants rushed to file and request examination under the old rules. [2]

### What makes the evidence persuasive?

- **U28 (descriptive)** found that Australians filed **1,044 standard patent applications in April 2013**, **4.41 times** their average month in the year before. [3]
- **B37 (observational)** compared the jump around the reform with jumps at other dates—“placebo months”, when the reform did not occur. Australians’ and overseas applicants’ standard patent filings both jumped further than in any of **72 placebo months**. The comparison series—Australians’ designs and plant breeder’s rights—did not show similarly unusual movements in that test. [4]
- **M25 (observational), the later-stage check, found that the rush holds** when each series’ trend and season are held together. Australians’ filings also showed a lower level afterwards—**about 28% fewer a month**—which then recovers. Most comparison series were quiet, although a rush in the small, noisy plant breeder’s rights series is a caution. [5]

### So, did the reforms cause it?

**My reading of this exploratory evidence is that it strongly supports applicants bringing filings forward ahead of the rule change**, rather than an ordinary monthly fluctuation: the timing is striking, the placebo comparisons support it, and the signal survives the trend-and-season check. [6] But holding those factors together is not an experiment; other unmeasured influences can still matter. The careful conclusion is **a robust observed rush consistent with a response to the reforms**, rather than a demonstrated causal effect.

events.answer:
**The evidence strongly supports a filing rush around Raising the Bar—but it does not establish causation.** Stage 3’s M25 (observational) found that the rush in Australians’ standard patent applications still stood out after accounting for the underlying trend and seasonal patterns.[1]

Raising the Bar tightened Australia’s patent law from **15 April 2013**, and applicants rushed to file and request examination under the old rules.[2] Here is how the atlas tested that pattern:

- **The initial observation:** Stage 1’s U28 (descriptive) recorded **1,044** Australian standard patent applications in **April 2013**, **4.41 times** the average month in the year before.[3]
- **The comparison test:** Stage 2’s B37 (observational) found that Australian and overseas standard patent filings both jumped further than in any of **72 placebo months**—comparison months used to check whether the jump was unusual.[4]
- **The stronger follow-up:** Stage 3’s M25 (observational) found that Australians’ rush held with trend and season accounted for, followed by a lower filing level—**about 28% fewer a month**—that subsequently recovered.[5] Comparison series were mostly quiet, although a rush in the small, noisy plant breeder’s rights series adds a caution.[6]

**My reading:** the timing, the unusual size of the rush and its survival under further checks make this persuasive evidence of applicants bringing filings forward around the rule change.[7] But accounting for trend and season is not an experiment: other influences could remain. The atlas therefore supports a strong observational conclusion, not a definitive claim that the reforms caused the rush.

evidence.title: What Stage 3 found
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text: - **The name match recovers most missing business numbers.** Tested on rights with a known ABN, 1.1% to 4.8% of matches name another ABN. Applied, it closes most of the recent fall in patents linked to an ABN and changes no firm finding. Adopting it is the owner's decision (OQ26). Observations: M12, U126.

evidence.title: M12: A name match to the business register recovers most missing business numbers accurately, and changes no firm finding
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
Matching Australian organisations' rights that have no filer's ABN to the ABR's and ASIC's names recovers a known ABN for 66% to 85% of rights where the ABN was hidden for a test, with 1.1% to 4.8% of matches naming another ABN. Applied to rights with no ABN it links 17.7% to 35.3% of them. It closes most of the recent fall in standard patents linked to an ABN, and moves concentration and the claimants' figures by less than a point.

- **The test:** standard patents FY2010 to FY2019, 83.41% matched and 81.70% recovered; FY2020 to FY2026, 68.95%, 67.85% and 1.60% another ABN. Trade marks 78.89%, 76.59% and 2.91%. Designs filed FY2000 to FY2009 are the weakest, 9.84% another ABN. A "wrong" ABN can be a related company of the same group.
- **With the postcode as well**, 42.62% to 46.04% matched, with 2.34% to 4.71% another ABN: it halves the matches for no gain in accuracy, so it was dropped.

evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text: **Name match (to the business register).** An ABN found for an Australian organisation's right that has none, by matching the filer's name to the ABR's main names and ASIC's company names, kept only if exactly one ABN has the name in the filer's state. Tested on rights with a known ABN; kept apart from the counts, never added to them (ADR 0045, 0047).

evidence.title: U126: The name match's columns are set only where they should be, and add 2% to 8% to the counts by ABN, concentrated in a few firms
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
The name match finds an ABN for 16.48% of Australian organisations' trade marks with no filer's ABN, and 28.95% of standard patents, but none of the plant breeder's rights. Counted by firm, the matched filings add 2.03% to the standard patents credited by ABN, 2.80% to trade marks and 7.59% to provisionals, concentrated in a few large organisations. They are kept apart, never added to the counts.

- **Where it is set:** empty outside its scope (0 rights). Of the rights with no filer's ABN, 31,960 of 193,879 trade marks (9,305 ABNs) and 4,116 of 14,219 standard patents (1,223 ABNs); 27.29% of provisionals, 20.67% of designs, 23.18% of second-tier patents, none of the 3,966 plant breeder's rights.
- **The four counts** have no empty values. Of the 948 ABNs with a standard patent found by name, 624 have none by ABN and 121 no filing linked at all; trade marks 7,561 ABNs and 28,547 applications, 2,594 with no filing linked.

evidence.text:
Every Australian Business Number that appears in IP RAPID, IP Australia's register, IPLORD, the R&D Tax Incentive, AusTender (government contracts) or the ATO's tax transparency reports, with what the business is, where it is registered, how old it is on the record, the IP it filed and holds, its R&D claims, its large-company income and its contracts. It is the businesses found in those sources, not every business in Australia, so a share of all businesses, or of all large employers, is taken over a wider count (B50). For employers of 100 or more, WGEA's reports add a size band and an industry; smaller firms have neither. Stage 3 added four counts of filings found by matching the filer's name to the business register, read beside the counts by ABN and never added to them (M12, U126).

evidence.title: U41: The firms table holds the businesses found in one of six sources, not every business, and its IP counts are lower bounds
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
- **Assumption:** An ABN stands for one business. Related companies in the same group have different ABNs and are counted separately.
- **Assumption:** A right with no ABN recorded for its filer cannot be credited to any firm; such rights are left out of firms' counts rather than guessed.
- **Limit:** The table is not a census of Australian businesses. A business found in none of the six sources is not in it, so rates worked out on this table are rates among these firms (U112 shows how much that matters).
- **Limit:** Firms' IP counts are lower bounds, because rights with no ABN (and IPLORD-only links) add nothing to them.

evidence.title: Limits and assumptions
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
The binding limit on what this research can say is how well its datasets link together. These are the links the two stages found weakest.

- **Firms.** Firms reach IP only through business numbers on applications, so firms' IP counts are lower bounds; IP RAPID's recent filings carry fewer, and IP Australia's register restores most for trade marks and designs (U41, U45, U100). A name match recovers most of the rest and changes no firm finding, but is kept apart from the counts (M12). Size and industry reach only employers of 100 or more (U112), the main third factor every firm signal lacks.
- **Industries.** Industries reach patents only through a crosswalk; the recommended one leaves out services, so a second one with services sits beside it (U75, U114).
- **Places.** Places reach IP only through postcodes, and half the universities' patents carry a postcode where no one lives (U49, U87).
- **Institutions.** Research institutions reach their IP through a reviewed list of names and business numbers that someone in the sector has yet to check (U81, OQ11).

evidence.text:
- **Review Stage 3's two tables**: the fifteen early signals and thirteen data gaps above, before the questions are answered.
- **The name match** (OQ26): whether to adopt the matched business numbers into the firms' counts, or keep them beside the counts (M12).
- **A sector check of the institutions link** (OQ11): a half-hour review by someone who knows the sector, which every institutions result rests on (M23, M24, M38).
- **Firms' size and industry for small firms** (OQ20): known only for employers of 100 or more; small firms need a paid or requested source.
- **Older Australian patent families** (OQ21): repair the links from the EPO's patent family service (free, but an account in your name), or read family measures from FY2010 only.

section: Step 4 of 4: From the data to the observation (5 reasoning steps)
pool.text:
The steps are not findings; only the last is.

1. Count the ABNs in the table, and for each, the sources it appears in.
2. Group the ABNs by that combination of sources and count each group.
3. For each group, work out the share whose ABN is still active in the business register.
4. For rights where both the filer's and the holder's ABN are known, count how often they differ.
5. Compare IPLORD's trade mark counts with IP RAPID's for the ABNs that appear in both.

**Which gives observation U41:** The table has 463,279 ABNs. 54.77% appear only because they filed IP in IP RAPID, 13.99% only because IP Australia's register links them to a trade mark or design, 11.55% only because they hold a government contract, and 10.96% only because an older IP Australia dataset (IPLORD) links them to IP. Anything measured across this table describes these firms, not Australian businesses in general.

pool.text:
- Public data are taken to be what their publishers say they are. Where checks found otherwise (placeholder dates, mislabelled countries, numbers counted twice), the data were repaired and the repair recorded; elsewhere, the publisher's values stand.
- A business is identified by its ABN. Related companies in a group have different ABNs and are counted apart.
- A place is a postal area, reached through the postcode recorded on an application or in the business register. A registered address may be a head office or an adviser's, not where the work is done.

- Money is shown as recorded (nominal) unless a page says otherwise; fees are also shown in June 2026 dollars, adjusted with the quarterly Consumer Price Index.
- Where a series begins with only the survivors of an earlier system, or with partial records, those years are left out rather than estimated.

section: For analysts: the notebook's own words

events.answer:
**Yes—matching firm names can recover missing Australian Business Numbers (ABNs), but not all of them.** Stage 3’s **M12 (descriptive)** recovered a known ABN for **66% to 85%** of rights in a test where the ABN was hidden; **1.1% to 4.8%** of matches named another ABN. Applied to rights whose ABN was genuinely missing, it linked **17.7% to 35.3%** of them.[1]

### How the matching works
The method matches the filer’s name against main names in the business register and company names. It keeps a match only when exactly one ABN has that name in the filer’s state, and applies to Australian organisations’ rights without a filer’s ABN.[2]

Testing against rights with a known ABN lets the researchers check whether the method finds the recorded number, rather than simply finding a plausible name match.[3] Adding postcode to the match was also tested, but it roughly halved the matches without improving accuracy, so that requirement was dropped.[4]

### Does it change the findings?
**It changes the picture of missing links much more than it changes the substantive firm findings.** M12 found that the match closes most of the recent fall in standard patents linked to an ABN, while moving concentration and the research and development claimants’ figures by less than a point.[5]

- **Recent patent links:** M12’s refinement of U45 shows that, with matched links, standard patents with an ABN go from **89.43% (FY2024)** to **89.20% (FY2026)**, compared with **88.68% to 83.85%** using the filer’s ABN alone. This suggests most of that recent fall reflects missing links rather than a comparable fall in linked firms’ patent activity.[6]
- **Concentration:** M12’s refinement of U44 leaves the pattern almost unchanged: the top **1%** of firms file **55.31%** of standard patents by ABN and **55.06%** with the matched links.[7]

### What are the limits?
The headline accuracy range is not universal: M12 found that designs filed **FY2000 to FY2009** were the weakest case, with **9.84%** of matches naming another ABN. A different ABN can also belong to a related company in the same group, rather than an entirely unrelated business.[8]

The method currently uses main business names and company names, not trading and business names, leaving a possible source of further matches unexplored.[9] More broadly, **U41 (descriptive)** treats firms’ IP counts as lower bounds because rights without a recorded ABN are left out rather than guessed.[10]

**The matched links are currently kept beside the original counts, not added to them.** Whether to adopt them into the firms’ counts remains a decision for the research owner.[11]

evidence.title: B29: Filing rises steeply with advantage and falls with remoteness; both hold when read together, in both halves of the areas
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
For each standard deviation of advantage (the IRSAD score), a postal area files 1.717 times as many standard patents per person (1.857 in the second half; 1.884 with areas pooled into larger SA3s). Inner regional areas file at 0.259 of major cities' rate. Read together, advantage's ratio is 1.442 and inner regional areas still file at 0.382 of the cities' rate at the same advantage (that combined reading was not repeated for SA3s).

- Trade marks 1.648 (1.707; 1.477), designs 1.504, provisionals 1.582. Very remote areas file standard patents at 0.173 of the cities' rate.
- **The shape is not a straight line:** standard patents run 0.33 to 0.75 a year per 10,000 people across deciles 1 to 8, then 1.51 to 1.62 in deciles 9 and 10. Most of the gradient is in the most advantaged fifth of areas; trade marks rise more steadily (7.63 to 29.24).
- The top tenth differs most between the halves (1.62 against 3.37 for standard patents) because its five heaviest filing areas, several of them mostly one firm's patents (U52), fall in the second half. Pooled rates there are fragile; the overall ratio is the steadier reading.

evidence.title: B58: Higher-income areas file more, and individuals there file more for each person who runs a business
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
Across postal areas (2023-24), taxable income per individual goes with standard patents per 10,000 people at a rank correlation of 0.384 and with trade marks at 0.453. The share of people with business income goes with filing far less (0.145 and 0.194). Individuals' own applications per 1,000 people with business income rise from a median 3.84 in the most disadvantaged tenth of areas to 11.0 in the most advantaged.

- The second half of the areas agrees: 0.405, 0.518, 0.229 and 0.212.
- Individuals' own filing per person in business barely moves with the share running a business (-0.078; -0.14).
- **So** the advantage gradient is not only that advantaged areas have more business owners.

evidence.title: Overview: what Australia's IP data show so far
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
- **Australian organisations' patents reach fewer countries; the signals of value disagree.** Filed in the same number of countries, Australian organisations' patents more often stay in force for 10 years than overseas organisations', except those filed only in Australia. But they reach fewer countries and are cited less, mostly because of that reach. Older Australian families' filings abroad are incomplete in the records, so these are read from FY2010. Observations: B8, B11, B12, B55.
- **Filing follows advantage and remoteness, not one firm.** Each step of area advantage goes with 1.7 to 1.9 times the standard patent rate, and the gradient holds with remoteness allowed for and with each area's largest filer taken out. Areas that gained graduates or income over a decade were not seen to gain filing, so it looks like a standing difference between places. Observations: B29, B30, B58, B59.

evidence.title: M14: Beyond advantage and remoteness, business density and places with more degrees than their resources suggest go with filing
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
With the four components and remoteness held together, the advantage gradient is still there but weaker: each standard deviation of advantage goes with 1.256 times the standard patent rate, against 1.932 with advantage alone (first half), so 35% to 39% of the raw ratio remains. Two other dimensions go with filing: business density, and degrees and R&D claimants beyond what an area's resources would suggest. Remoteness stays.

- **Trade marks:** 1.830 and 1.362, 51% left (holds, just); 1.988 and 1.386, 48% (weakened). **Designs:** 1.863 and 1.186. **Provisionals:** 1.652 and 1.247. Weakened.
- **Held together, for standard patents:** the second component (older areas, small households, many businesses) 1.446 and 1.219; the third 0.731 and 0.663, so areas with more degrees and R&D claimants than their resources would suggest file more; the fourth 0.702 and 0.666. The same signs for trade marks, designs and provisionals.
- **Remoteness stays:** very remote areas file standard patents at 0.218 and 0.115 of major cities' rate.

evidence.title: What comes next
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
section: Early signals that warrant further investigation
evidence.text:
- **Among R&D claimants, older firms, higher spenders and public companies more often have a standard patent linked, held together; among suppliers, company form, age and a city address (not the postcode's advantage); suppliers that file win more contracts and value; among large employers the size gap widens within industry; large taxpayers that file report no more income.** Observations: B22, B23, B24, B50, B51, M8, M9, M11, M12, M29. Strength: Observational. Questions: Q2, Q3, Q4. Next: Firm size and industry for small firms (OQ20); the timing of filing against contracts and claims.
- **Filing concentrates in advantaged, educated city areas, and beyond the advantage gradient goes with business density, degrees and R&D claimants beyond what resources predict, and manufacturing's share of businesses (where Stage 2 saw none); remoteness stays; most attached indicators are the gradient.** Observations: B27, B28, B29, B30, B31, M13, M14, M15, M16, M31, M32. evidence.text:
Stage 2 answers none of the five questions either: it finds which measures go together. This is how the association prepares the ground for them.

- **Q2. Who benefits, and who is underserved?** Filing follows one broad gradient of place advantage, so who benefits from IP is tied to where people live.

evidence.title: B59: Areas that gained graduates or income over the decade to 2021 were not seen to gain filing
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
The median area's share of people with a bachelor degree or higher rose 5.9 points from 2011 to 2021, and its residents' standard patents per person fell. Gaining graduates goes with the change in filing at -0.065 (patents) and -0.104 (trade marks); gaining income at -0.081 and -0.016. All are small (at most 0.147 in size, in either half of the areas) and all negative: no association detected.

- The median area's income rose about 39% (dollars of the day); its patents per person fell, and its trade marks rose slightly.
- The 2011 share of graduates against the later change: -0.024 and -0.065 (-0.063 and -0.147 in the second half).
- **So** levels go together (B29, B58) but changes were not seen to: the advantage gradient looks like a standing difference between places, not one that moves with them. That is not evidence that education or income has no effect.

evidence.text:
Across 2,525 postal areas, the measures of advantage, income and education can largely be predicted from one another. Summarised as components, the first, an advantage gradient on which every advantage measure rises together, carries 49.5% of the variation; the first four carry 82.3%. So Stage 2's single indicators (income, education, advantage) are mostly one measure: none should be read as the one that matters.

evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
- **Fees look a weak lever.** Owners did not let rights go more often at the anniversary after any of nine renewal fee changes (for patents, within about 1.4 points either way), and with trend and season held most filing fee breaks do not behave as prices would. Observations: M28, M34.
- **Among firms, age, form and size go with filing; R&D spend only weakly.** Older R&D claimants and public companies more often have a filing linked, held together; government suppliers that file win about two and a half times the contracts; among large employers the size gap widens within an industry. Spending above the median goes with a standard patent by only 4 to 5 points. Observations: M8, M9, M11, M29.

Beyond it, business density, manufacturing businesses and places with more degrees than their resources suggest go with filing; residents' incomes add nothing detectable; remoteness stays. section: Step 3 of 4: How it was prepared (1 step for this observation, on the places lens)
pool.text:
**For this observation**

1. Australian standard patents filed FY2017 to FY2026, placed by the filer's postcode, with the largest filer in each area taken by the filer's party, whether or not it has an ABN.
   - _Why:_ The same party that gives the patent its postcode, as the final review asked.

**Repairs made to the places lens before any observation**

1. Applications are counted at the filer's postcode, not the current holder's.
   - _Why:_ A right sold to a firm elsewhere should stay where it was filed.
2. A rate is shown only where 10 or more applications would be expected at the national rate.
   - _Why:_ A count of 10 has a 95% range of about 5 to 18 by chance alone; below that, an area's rate is mostly noise.
3. Small areas can be pooled into 335 larger ones (SA3s).
   - _Why:_ So that every area's filings count somewhere, even where its own rate is too uncertain to show.
4. Values published for other kinds of area are moved to postal areas by their 2021 residents.
   - _Why:_ A count can be split by where people live; a median or rate is averaged, weighted by the people shared.

pool.text:
Besides testing signals, Stage 3 asked which measures repeat each other and whether there are distinct kinds of place or country. These are descriptive.

- **Places' characteristics are mostly one advantage gradient.** Across 2,525 postal areas the first component, advantage, carries 49.5% of the variation, and IRSAD can be predicted almost entirely from the other measures. No single measure (income, education) should be read as the one that matters. Observations: M13.
- **Places form a continuum, not kinds.** The best grouping of areas has a silhouette of 0.269, short of clear segments; one group of 288 advantaged, educated city areas holds 56% of the placed standard patents. Observations: M16.

pool.text:
18 changes of 10% or more in the cost of obtaining a right (12 rises, 6 cuts) were set against placebo months: 34 pairs of a change and a filing series. Five moved filing beyond 95% of their placebo months (three rushes and two steps), against about 1.7 of each expected by chance. Only one of the five moved the way a price would: Australians' designs fell after the rise of July 1988. The clearest breaks came with new Acts, the Trade Marks Act 1995 and the Designs Act 2003.

- **How a price would push:** filing brought forward before a rise and lower after it; before a cut, filing would wait, and rise after it.
- **The Trade Marks Act 1995** (January 1996): filing by Australians and overseas applicants fell before the rise (2.778% of placebo months as large), which is the Act's pause (B37), not a price.
- **Overseas applicants' standard patents** were filed early before the 15.31% cut of January 1998 (2.778%), the opposite of what a price would do.
- **The Designs Act 2003** (June 2004, a design's filing fee up 122.2%): overseas applicants' designs stepped up (none of 72 placebo months as large), against a price; that is the Act (B37).

events.answer:
**Yes—more advantaged postal areas tend to file more standard patents per person.** The link remains when other area characteristics are held together, but it becomes weaker: that is the observational finding of Stage 3’s **M14**.[1]

### How strong is the pattern?
**B29 (Stage 2, observational)** found that each standard-deviation step up in area advantage went with **1.717 times** the standard patent filing rate per person.[2] A standard deviation is a way of expressing a step in advantage relative to how widely areas differ.

The pattern was not a steady climb: standard patent rates ranged from **0.33 to 0.75 a year per 10,000 people** across advantage deciles **1 to 8**, then reached **1.51 to 1.62** in deciles **9 and 10**—so most of the gradient was concentrated in the most advantaged fifth of areas.[3]

### What did Stage 3 change?
**M13 (descriptive)** found that advantage, income and education overlap heavily, so they should not be read as separate explanations of filing.[4] **M14 (observational)** then held broader area characteristics and remoteness together: the standard patent rate ratio fell from **1.932** with advantage alone to **1.256** per standard deviation of advantage in the first half of areas—an outcome of **weakened**, rather than disappearing.[1] Business density and places with more degrees and research and development (R&D) claimants than their resources would suggest also went with filing; remoteness remained relevant.[5]

### What does that mean—and not mean?
- **It is not simply one big filer in each advantaged area.** Stage 3’s **M15 (observational)** found that the advantage gradient was steeper after each area’s largest filer was removed.[6]
- **It does not show that becoming more advantaged causes filing to rise.** **B59 (Stage 2, observational)** detected no association between gains in graduates or income over the decade to 2021 and gains in filing; it read the gradient as a standing difference between places, while explicitly warning that this is not evidence that education or income has no effect.[7]

So the evidence supports a clear difference **between places**, not a demonstrated causal effect of advantage on patent filing.[8]

events.answer:
**Yes—more advantaged postal areas generally file more standard patents per person.** B29 (observational) found a strong association, and Stage 3’s M14 (observational) found that it remains, but is weaker, when other area characteristics and remoteness are held together.[1]

### How strong is the pattern?
- **B29:** Each standard deviation—a standard-sized step—of the area advantage score goes with **1.717 times** the standard patent filing rate per person. With remoteness also held together, the ratio is **1.442**.[2]
- **The pattern is steepest at the advantaged end.** B29 found that most of the difference is in the most advantaged fifth of areas, rather than filing rising evenly across the whole range.[3]
- **It is not just a few dominant filers.** Stage 3’s M15 (observational) found that the advantage–filing relationship is steeper after removing each area’s largest filer, confirming the earlier finding with a better-aligned way of identifying those filers.[4]

### What did Stage 3 add?
M13 (descriptive) found that advantage, income and education largely overlap: they should not be treated as separate explanations, or any one of them as the factor that matters.[5]

M14 then held those overlapping characteristics and remoteness together. Using its combined advantage measure, the standard patent rate ratio fell from **1.932** with advantage alone to **1.256** with the other factors held together in the first half of areas. Its outcome was **weakened, not removed**; business density and having more degrees and research and development claimants than an area’s resources would suggest also went with filing.[6]

### What does that mean?
The safest reading is a **persistent difference between places, not proof that becoming more advantaged makes a place file more patents**. B59 (observational) found no detectable association between areas gaining graduates or income and changes in filing; it explicitly cautions that this is not evidence that education or income has no effect.[7] Holding measured factors together also cannot rule out explanations the analysis has not measured.

So Stage 2's single indicators (income, education, advantage) are mostly one measure: none should be read as the one that matters.

claims.text: M14 then held those overlapping characteristics and remoteness together. Using its combined advantage measure, the standard patent rate ratio fell from 1.932 with advantage alone to 1.256 with the other factors held together in the first half of areas. Its outcome was weakened, not removed; business density and having more degrees and research and development claimants than an area’s resources would suggest also went with filing.

citations.quote: With the four components and remoteness held together, the advantage gradient is still there but weaker: each standard deviation of advantage goes with 1.256 times the standard patent rate, against 1.932 with advantage alone (first half), so 35% to 39% of the raw ratio remains.
Two other dimensions go with filing: business density, and degrees and R&D claimants beyond what an area's resources would suggest.

claims.text: The safest reading is a persistent difference between places, not proof that becoming more advantaged makes a place file more patents. B59 (observational) found no detectable association between areas gaining graduates or income and changes in filing; it explicitly cautions that this is not evidence that education or income has no effect.

citations.quote: Gaining graduates goes with the change in filing at -0.065 (patents) and -0.104 (trade marks); gaining income at -0.081 and -0.016.
All are small (at most 0.147 in size, in either half of the areas) and all negative: no association detected.
- **So** levels go together (B29, B58) but changes were not seen to: the advantage gradient looks like a standing difference between places, not one that moves with them.
That is not evidence that education or income has no effect.

evidence.title: M40: Asking for examination before being directed goes with patents more likely to end, not less, against IP Australia's commissioned study
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
IP Australia's commissioned study counts a request for examination made before the Commissioner directs one as a way of speeding examination up, and reports that applicants who speed up are more likely to renew their patents. Built from the open data, the same measure covers 41.39% of granted patents (the study: 41.9%). But with the filer, field, route, cohort and expedited examination held together, those patents are more likely to end in a given year after grant, in both periods (hazard ratios 1.276 and 1.383).

- **The measure reproduces the study's share:** 303,486 standard patents with a date of patent in 2004 to 2016, divisionals left out, of which 191,477 granted; 41.28% were never directed. The share rose between the periods: overseas organisations 0.273 to 0.5148, Australian organisations 0.2357 to 0.4602.
- **By filer, held together:** overseas organisations 1.282, then 1.388; overseas individuals 1.298, then 1.340; Australian organisations 1.005 (not detected either way), then 1.587; Australian individuals 1.169 (not detected once held), then 1.486.

**For this observation**

**Repairs made to the IP rights lens before any observation**

1. Where a right's applicants have no country recorded, its origin is "unknown", not "overseas".

**M40 found that patents whose applicants requested examination before being directed to do so were more likely to end after grant—not less likely.** This is a Stage 3 **observational** finding: the link remained when the filer, technology field, filing route, cohort and expedited examination were held together.[1]

### What the analysis found
M40 used the same broad measure of speeding up examination as IP Australia’s commissioned study: requesting examination before any direction from the Commissioner. It reproduced a very similar share—**41.39%** of granted standard patents, **2004 to 2016**, compared with the study’s **41.9%**.[2]

But the relationship with patent survival went the other way. After holding the other factors together, the hazard ratios for patents ending were:
- **1.276** for **FY2010 to FY2016**.[3]
- **1.383** for **FY2003 to FY2009**.[4]

A hazard ratio above one means a higher likelihood of ending at a given point among patents still in force. M40 followed each patent from grant, comparing patents alive at the same age.[5]

### Why that matters—and what remains uncertain
M40 **refined the earlier B13 signal**: on the commissioned study’s wider measure, it did not find the reported link between speeding up examination and a longer patent life.[6] The atlas therefore labels the comparison **“disputed in part”**: it challenges the direction of the study’s result on this measure, but cannot test the study’s model because its outcome definition and model are not published in IP Australia’s report.[7]

One possible explanation—not an established finding—is that applicants who wait have more time to drop weaker applications before grant, leaving a more selected group of granted patents among those who were directed to request examination.[8] Holding measured factors together does not make this a causal result: it does **not** establish that requesting examination early makes a patent end sooner.

The proposed next check is to ask IP Australia exactly how the commissioned study measured renewal lifetime and which factors it held together.[9]

evidence.title: B6: Patents that Australian individuals file without an attorney are rarely granted, about 36 points less often, in both decades
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
Of the standard patents Australian individuals filed alone in FY2010 to FY2019, 4.8% were granted, against 40.6% of those filed with an attorney: a gap of 35.8 points (interval 33.9 to 37.5). In FY2000 to FY2009 the gap was 36.8 points. It stays among applications whose examination was requested (34.4 points).

- **Filing alone goes with not asking for examination:** 25.2% of individuals' lone applications were examined, against 75.9% with an attorney.
- **Australian organisations do not show it in both decades:** a gap of 40.0 points in FY2010 to FY2019 but -6.0 in FY2000 to FY2009, when the 1,149 applications organisations filed alone were granted 62.1% of the time. Those earlier lone filers may have been firms with their own patent staff; the data do not say.
- **Trade marks show it in both decades, for both:** with an attorney, Australian individuals' marks are registered 24.3 points more often, organisations' 23.6 points.

evidence.title: B6: Patents that Australian individuals file without an attorney are rarely granted, about 36 points less often, in both decades
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
- **Designs cannot be read here:** the comparison keeps only designs with a known filer, and IP RAPID gives no origin for nearly every design that lapsed or was withdrawn (B3), so its 99.4% to 100% registered reflects that selection, not designs' registration rate.
- **Not a cause.** Representation counts an agent recorded at any time, so an application dropped early may never appoint one (the arrow can run backwards); and those who file alone differ in resources and experience.

Stage 3's first table, for the research owner's review (section 8 of the Stage 3 notebook). Each signal is an association that survived its third factors held together, in both samples unless marked; none is a cause, and adopting any as a conclusion is the owner's decision.

- **Filing alone goes with far fewer grants (Australian individuals' standard patents, about 31 points), and no agent before the first renewal with fewer trade marks and designs in force after it, with the factors settled at filing held.** Observations: B5, B6, B10, M1, M2. Now: Each now has its test (M26 to M38); two figures were corrected where they stood (M1's verdict, M16's lowest silhouette), and the labour market and the IP judgments, planned for the timeline, were attached (U124, B63).
